--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/case-study-under-the-rug/ title: "Under the Rug" summary: "Your startup is marketing a product you know does not work, and your manager says keep quiet." ---

After graduation from UIC, you accept a well-paying job at a fast-growing technology startup that has raised millions of dollars in funding. You make a good salary, your benefits are excellent (401k, healthcare, and generous parental leave!), and you work on a small, friendly team with a dozen other people.

After two years of working there, the company decides its product is ready for marketing to customers. However, you have discovered that the product does not yet work as marketed. Internal tests consistently suggest issues with the product which could mislead users and/or cause real harm if deployed to the real world. You discuss these issues with your team, your managers, and even company executives, but they dismiss the concerns and continue promoting the product. Your manager warns you not to discuss the issues outside the company.

What are your options? What would you do?

Source: Erika Cheung and Tyler Shultz

See also: the SEP page on Business Ethics, 6.4 "Whistleblowing" (uses the Tyler Shultz/Theranos case cited above)

See also: the SEP page on Loyalty, 6.1 "Whistle blowing"

See also: Adam Waytz, James Dungan, and Liane Young, "The whistleblower's dilemma and the fairness–loyalty tradeoff", Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 49, no. 6 (2013): 1027–1033 — experiments suggesting that people who value fairness over loyalty are more willing to report wrongdoing, and that priming either value can shift the decision.

See also: James Dungan, Adam Waytz, and Liane Young, "The psychology of whistleblowing", Current Opinion in Psychology 6 (2015): 129–133 — a review of what predicts whether someone speaks up.
